questions.q: What module does this course use to give PowerShell the ability to talk to Azure?
options: Az
AzureCore
PSAzure
PowerShell talks to Azure natively with no module required
questions.explain: Az is the current standard module for managing Azure resources from PowerShell.

questions.q: What is AzureRM, and why does it matter to know about it?
options: It's the retired predecessor to Az — seeing it in a script online is a sign that script is old and needs updating
It's a completely unrelated module for managing on-premises servers only
It's a newer, more advanced replacement for Az released after this course
It's a required companion module that must be installed alongside Az
questions.explain: Microsoft retired AzureRM in favor of Az; recognizing AzureRM in an old script is a real, practical signal.

questions.q: Why is -Scope CurrentUser usually the right choice when installing Az?
options: It installs the module for your account only and usually doesn't require administrator rights, unlike -Scope AllUsers
It installs a smaller, limited version of Az with fewer cmdlets
It is required for Az to connect to Azure at all
It only works with the AzureRM module, not Az
questions.explain: CurrentUser scoping avoids the elevated-prompt requirement that AllUsers scoping needs.

questions.q: What naming pattern do Az cmdlets follow, and why does it matter?
options: Verb-Az<Service><Noun>, e.g. Get-AzSqlServer — once you know the pattern, guessing a cmdlet name gets easier
Az cmdlets have no consistent naming pattern at all
Az<Service>-Verb-Noun, with the service name always first
All Az cmdlets are named identically regardless of what they do
questions.explain: The pattern extends the Verb-Noun convention from Lesson 3 with an Az<Service> segment in the middle.

questions.q: What does Get-InstalledModule -Name Az -ListAvailable do, and when is it worth running?
options: It confirms what's actually installed on a machine — worth checking before assuming Az is ready, especially on a machine you didn't set up yourself
It installs the Az module automatically if it's missing
It connects directly to an Azure subscription
It uninstalls any outdated version of AzureRM
questions.explain: It's a check, not an install or connect action — useful before relying on Az being present.
